chapters.title: Chapter 5: Valuation in Indian Corporate Practice

lessons.title: Valuation Rules for ESOPs, Fundraises and Share Transfers: Rule 11UA, FEMA and SEBI Pricing

children.text: Lesson 5.1 answered who signs. This lesson answers what the number has to be. Indian law rarely tells you what a business is worth. It tells you the floor you may not go below, or the ceiling you may not go above, depending on who is on the other side of the transaction and which law is asking. Get those boundaries wrong and the transaction is not merely mispriced, it is non-compliant.

body.text: Regulatory valuation rules do not produce a value. They produce a boundary. Your negotiated price still has to be defensible commercially, and it also has to sit on the right side of every boundary that applies to that particular transaction.

children.text: The Income Tax Rules: Rule 11UA

Rule 11UA of the Income-tax Rules prescribes how the fair market value of unquoted shares is computed for income tax purposes. For unquoted equity shares, the default is a net asset value calculation, with specified assets substituted at prescribed values rather than book value.

body.latex: \text{FMV per share} = \frac{\text{Adjusted assets} - \text{Liabilities}}{\text{Number of equity shares}}
body.caption: The net asset value route, simplified. The rule prescribes specific substitutions and exclusions for particular assets and liabilities

children.text: Immovable property
is taken at stamp duty value rather than book value.
Shares and securities held
are taken at their own fair market value, worked out under the same rules.
Jewellery, artistic work and similar assets
are taken at open market value.
Certain items are excluded from liabilities
, such as paid-up capital and provisions for unascertained liabilities, so they do not artificially depress the value.

body.title: Run the net asset value route
body.prompt: A company has adjusted assets of ₹120 crore and liabilities of ₹70 crore, with 50 lakh equity shares in issue. What is the fair market value per share, in rupees?
body.explanation: ₹120 crore - ₹70 crore = ₹50 crore. Divided by 50 lakh shares, that is ₹100 a share. Notice how mechanical this is: the answer falls out of the balance sheet. That is precisely why a growing startup with few assets and a large future can produce a very low fair market value on this route, which is why the discounted cash flow alternative matters so much to founders.

children.text: The rule was widened in September 2023. Alongside net asset value and discounted cash flow, five further methods became available for issues to non-resident investors: comparable company multiple, probability weighted expected return, option pricing, milestone analysis and replacement cost. The amendment also allowed a merchant banker's report dated up to 90 days before the date of issue to be used.

body.text: The provision that made these valuations so contentious, commonly called angel tax, was abolished for all classes of investors from assessment year 2025-26. The valuation machinery survived its abolition. Fair market value under these rules still matters for other charges, including where a person receives shares for less than fair market value, and it still sits alongside the FEMA requirement.

children.text: FEMA: Floors and Ceilings by Direction of Money

Exchange control pricing has one organising idea: the non-resident must not get a better deal than fair value at the expense of the Indian side. Which way the rule points depends on which way the shares are moving.

body.caption: FEMA pricing for unlisted Indian company shares

cells: Company issues shares to a non-resident
Price must not be less than fair value
Foreign money must not buy Indian equity cheaply
Resident transfers shares to a non-resident
Price must not be less than fair value
Same principle, applied to a secondary sale
Non-resident transfers shares to a resident
Price must not exceed fair value
Money leaving India must not leave at an inflated price
Who certifies
Chartered accountant, SEBI registered Category I merchant banker, or practising cost accountant
Internationally accepted pricing methodology on an arm's length basis
How long the certificate lasts
90 days from the date of the certificate
A delayed closing needs a fresh certificate

body.title: Which way does the rule point?
body.question: A Mauritius fund wants to sell its entire stake in an unlisted Indian company back to the Indian promoters. The valuation certificate puts fair value at ₹420 a share. The parties have negotiated ₹460. What is the problem?
options: None, because a negotiated price between willing parties always prevails
The price exceeds fair value on a transfer from a non-resident to a resident, which the pricing rules do not permit
The price is too low, because a non-resident must always receive a premium
The certificate is irrelevant once the parties have agreed a price
body.explanation: When shares move from a non-resident to a resident, the price must not exceed fair value, because that is money leaving India. At ₹460 against a fair value of ₹420, the transaction as structured does not comply. The fix is either to transact at or below fair value, or to obtain a fresh, properly supported valuation that genuinely justifies a higher figure.

children.text: SEBI: Pricing a Preferential Issue in a Listed Company

For listed companies the market supplies the price, so the rules work off traded prices rather than a valuer's opinion. For a preferential issue of frequently traded shares, the floor price is the higher of the volume weighted average price over the 90 trading days and over the 10 trading days preceding the relevant date, and the price arrived at under any valuation method prescribed in the issuer's articles of association.

stats.label: Floor price
stats.value: Higher of 90 and 10 trading day VWAP
stats.context: Plus any method prescribed in the articles

body.title: Find the floor price
body.prompt: A listed company plans a preferential allotment. The volume weighted average price over the preceding 90 trading days is ₹180 and over the preceding 10 trading days is ₹196. Its articles prescribe no separate method. What is the floor price per share, in rupees?
body.explanation: The floor is the higher of the two, so ₹196. The 10 day figure catches a recent run-up in the price, which stops an allotment being priced off a stale three month average after good news has already moved the stock. The company may issue above the floor, never below it.

body.text: The relevant date, from which those windows are counted backwards, is defined in the regulations and is tied to the meeting at which shareholders approve the issue. Getting the relevant date wrong shifts both averages and can invalidate the pricing. This is a compliance question for the company secretary, not a judgment call.

children.text: ESOPs: Three Valuations, Two Taxes
Employee options are the place where valuation rules touch the most people in a company, and where the arithmetic is most often explained badly.

body.caption: The life of one employee option

cells: Grant
The exercise price fixed by the board, usually with reference to a valuation
No tax at this stage
Exercise
Fair market value on the exercise date, from a Category I merchant banker for unlisted shares
The excess over the exercise price is taxed as a salary perquisite
Sale
The price actually received
Capital gains are computed from the fair market value already taxed as perquisite

children.text: The charge sits in the salary provisions. The value of specified securities or sweat equity shares allotted free of cost or at a concessional rate is a perquisite under Section 17(1)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [Section 17(2)(vi) of the Income-tax Act, 1961], and the computation, fair market value on the date of exercise less the amount paid by the employee, sits in Section 17(5)(h).

body.caption: Worked example: 4,000 options in an unlisted company

cells: Exercise price paid by the employee
₹2,00,000 paid out of pocket
Fair market value on the exercise date
Merchant banker's report
Perquisite taxed as salary
₹10,00,000 added to salary income
Sale price two years later
Capital gain
₹8,00,000, computed from the ₹300 already taxed

body.text: The employee pays ₹2,00,000 to exercise and is taxed on ₹10,00,000 of salary in the same year, in cash, while holding shares that may have no buyer. Employees of eligible startups can defer the deduction of tax on this perquisite under Section 392(3) read with Section 289(3) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [Section 192(1C) of the Income-tax Act, 1961], but the eligibility conditions are narrow. Every HR team running an ESOP scheme should model this cash impact before employees exercise, not after.

body.title: Compute the capital gain
body.prompt: Using the example above, an employee exercises 4,000 options at ₹50 when fair market value is ₹300, and sells two years later at ₹500. What is the total capital gain, in rupees?
body.explanation: 4,000 × (₹500 - ₹300) = ₹8,00,000. The cost for capital gains purposes is the ₹300 fair market value already taxed as a perquisite, not the ₹50 actually paid. Without that rule the employee would be taxed twice on the same ₹250 a share.

children.text: When Several Rules Apply at Once
A single share issue can face more than one boundary. They do not cancel each other out. Each applies on its own terms, and the price has to satisfy all of them simultaneously.

columns.label: What each rule controls
points: Companies Act: a registered valuer's report supporting the issue price
FEMA: a floor, when the investor is a non-resident
Income tax: fair market value, which decides whether anyone is taxed on receiving shares cheaply
SEBI, for listed issuers: a formula floor from traded prices

columns.label: How to work through it
points: List every rule that the specific transaction triggers
Establish the boundary each one sets, and its direction
Price at or above the highest applicable floor, and below any applicable ceiling
Document why the commercial price also makes sense, because compliance is not the same as a defensible valuation

body.text: Notice the asymmetry that catches people out. FEMA sets a floor for money coming in and a ceiling for money going out. Income tax worries about someone receiving shares below fair market value. SEBI worries about a listed company issuing shares too cheaply to a favoured party. Each rule is protecting a different party, which is exactly why they can point in different directions.

body.title: The quarter from hell
body.scenario: You are the CFO of an unlisted Chennai analytics company. This quarter: a Dubai-based family office is investing ₹60 crore for fresh equity; two Indian angels are converting notes issued 18 months ago; the board wants to grant fresh ESOPs at an exercise price of ₹40 when the round price is ₹310; and a founder wants to sell some of her own shares to the incoming investor as a secondary. The last valuation report on file is dated four months ago.
body.prompt: Map out what valuation work is required and what could go wrong.
body.modelAnswer:
What is required:
1. The fresh issue to the Dubai investor triggers FEMA pricing. The issue price must not be below fair value certified by a chartered accountant, Category I merchant banker or practising cost accountant, and that certificate must be current when the shares are allotted.
2. The same issue triggers the Companies Act requirement for a registered valuer's report supporting the price, in the securities or financial assets class.
3. Income tax fair market value under the prescribed rules needs to be established for the issue, with the report dated within the permitted window before the issue.
4. The founder's secondary sale to a non-resident is a transfer from a resident to a non-resident, so the price must not be below fair value. It is a separate transaction with its own pricing test, and it has its own tax consequences for the founder.
5. The note conversion needs to be checked against the terms of the instrument and the prices at which shares are being issued in the same round, since a conversion at a discount raises questions about why other parties paid more.
6. The ESOP grant at ₹40 against a round price of ₹310 needs a defensible basis, and the exercise valuation later will be a separate merchant banker exercise.

What could go wrong:
7. The four month old report is already outside the 90 day windows. Anyone relying on it is relying on an expired document.
8. Different reports concluding different values for the same quarter, with no explanation. Differences are defensible when the purpose or the date differs. Unexplained differences are not.
9. The ₹40 exercise price sitting far below a contemporaneous ₹310 round price will be questioned by the auditor and by any future acquirer, and it also enlarges the perquisite the employees will eventually be taxed on.
10. Closing slipping past the validity of the certificates, which is the single most common failure in Indian rounds.

What I would do first: fix the target closing date, then work backwards and commission every report so that none expires before allotment, and keep one file with each report, its purpose, its signatory and its expiry date.

body.title: The direction of the rule
body.textWithBlank: When a non-resident transfers shares in an unlisted Indian company to a resident, the price must not ___ the fair value certified under the FEMA pricing rules.
body.explanation: Money leaving India must not leave at an inflated price. In the opposite direction, when a resident sells to a non-resident, the price must not be below fair value.

body.title: Pricing a transaction under Indian rules
steps: Identify every rule the transaction triggers: Companies Act, FEMA, income tax, SEBI
For each, note whether it sets a floor or a ceiling, and on which date it is tested
Commission the right report from the right professional for each purpose
Check the validity window of each certificate against the expected closing date
Price at or above the highest floor and below any ceiling that applies
Record why the commercial price is defensible, separately from why it is compliant
For ESOP grants, model the perquisite tax employees will face at exercise before fixing the exercise price
Keep one file with each report, its purpose, its date and its signatory

body.label: SEBI: ICDR Regulations and circulars
body.description: The source for preferential issue pricing, the definition of the relevant date and the frequently traded test. Check for amendments before relying on any summary, including this one.

cards.definition: The income tax rule prescribing how fair market value of unquoted shares is computed.
The default method under the rule: adjusted assets less liabilities, divided by shares.
Shares issued or transferred to a non-resident must be priced at or above fair value.
Shares transferred from a non-resident to a resident must be priced at or below fair value.
The date defined in the SEBI regulations from which the VWAP windows for a preferential issue are counted back.
Shares whose turnover over 240 trading days is at least 10% of total shares.
Fair market value on the exercise date less the amount paid by the employee, taxed as salary.
For ESOP shares, the fair market value already taxed as a perquisite, not the exercise price.

points: Indian valuation rules set boundaries, not values. The commercial number still has to be defended separately.
Rule 11UA computes fair market value of unquoted shares, with net asset value as the default and further methods available, including five added in September 2023 for non-resident investors.

FEMA sets a floor when shares go to a non-resident and a ceiling when they come back from one, certified by a chartered accountant, Category I merchant banker or practising cost accountant, valid 90 days.
For a listed preferential issue of frequently traded shares, the floor is the higher of the 90 and 10 trading day VWAP, counted back from the relevant date.
An ESOP is valued three times: at grant, at exercise for the salary perquisite under Section 17(1)(d) of the Income-tax Act, 2025 [Section 17(2)(vi) of the 1961 Act], and at sale for capital gains.
In the worked example, 4,000 options at ₹50 with fair market value of ₹300 produced ₹10,00,000 of salary perquisite, and a later sale at ₹500 produced ₹8,00,000 of capital gain.
When several rules apply at once, the price must satisfy all of them, and every certificate must still be within its validity window on the closing date.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not legal, tax or investment advice. Rules are summarised in outline, carry exceptions and conditions not covered here, and change through amendments, notifications and Finance Acts. The company in the scenario is fictional. Take professional advice on any actual transaction, and confirm the current position before relying on any figure or window mentioned here.
